nameStory: The cinnamon-fruited dandelion gets its name from its distinctive rust-colored or cinnamon-brown seeds, which set it apart from the common white-plumed dandelion seeds we all know. While most dandelions have pale, fluffy seed heads, this species produces seeds with a warm, reddish-brown color that resembles the spice cinnamon.
description: The cinnamon-fruited dandelion is a small perennial herb that looks very similar to the common dandelion at first glance. It produces the familiar yellow, daisy-like flowers and grows in a low rosette of deeply-lobed leaves radiating from the center. The plant typically reaches 4-8 inches tall when flowering, with leaves that can spread 6-12 inches across. What makes this dandelion special is revealed only when it goes to seed, producing those telltale cinnamon-colored fruits.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Seeds are distinctly cinnamon-brown to rust-colored rather than the pale straw color of common dandelions. The fluffy white pappus (the parachute part) contrasts beautifully with the darker seed body.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads composed of many small ray petals, identical in appearance to common dandelions. Flowers are about 1-2 inches across and sit atop hollow, leafless stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply lobed, tooth-edged leaves form a basal rosette. Leaves feel smooth to slightly rough and have a bitter, milky sap when broken, just like other dandelions.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing rosette pattern with all leaves emerging from ground level. Flower stems are hollow and contain milky white latex that will stain fingers when broken.

habitat: This rare dandelion prefers disturbed soils, roadsides, and waste places, similar to common dandelions but seemingly much less adaptable. In New England, it's been found in areas with sandy or gravelly soil. Given its extreme rarity here, it may prefer slightly different soil conditions or climate than our abundant common dandelion.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early and flowers begin blooming in late spring, typically May. Fresh green rosettes are most visible as other vegetation is just starting to grow.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in early summer, followed by seed development. The distinctive cinnamon-colored seeds are most evident in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Plants may produce a second flush of flowers in early fall. Leaves remain green and can be identified through autumn.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to root crown in harsh winters, though some leaves may persist in protected locations. Not identifiable above ground during coldest months.

funFact: With only one recorded observation in all of New England, the cinnamon-fruited dandelion is exponentially rarer here than finding a four-leaf clover - you're literally more likely to win the lottery than stumble across one of these botanical needles in our regional haystack!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from common dandelion until seeds develop - the cinnamon-colored fruits are the only reliable field mark. Memory trick: 'Cinnamon color = cinnamon-fruited' - if the seeds aren't distinctly brownish, it's just a regular dandelion.
contextualKnowledge: This species demonstrates how even 'weedy' plant families like dandelions can harbor rare and poorly understood species. Many people assume all yellow composite flowers in disturbed areas are common dandelions, but careful observation of seed characteristics can reveal botanical surprises.
compareHints: Among New England dandelions, only the cinnamon-fruited dandelion has distinctly brown seeds - common dandelion and red-seeded dandelion both have much paler, straw-colored to light brown fruits. Red-seeded dandelion seeds may have a slight reddish tinge, but nothing approaching the rich cinnamon-brown of this species. Fen dandelion is restricted to wetland habitats and also lacks the distinctive seed coloration.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common dandelion is much more widespread than its relatives in New England.
Red-seeded dandelion is most easily distinguished from common dandelion by its reddish seeds rather than pale yellow ones.
Fen dandelion differs from common dandelion primarily in its exclusive wetland habitat and potentially smaller, more delicate features.
